question: We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
must_cover: Start visible language now: sign to the baby even before the parents are fluent
Contact the state early intervention program (IDEA Part C) to begin services
Every day of accessible language exposure in the first year protects the critical period
Ask for bilingual-bimodal services and a Deaf mentor
The diagnosis is not the parents' fault and the tone stays supportive, not blaming
must_not: Wait and see whether hearing technology works before starting sign language
Blame or shame the parents for anything they did or did not do
Present deafness as a tragedy with no path forward

question: Our audiologist says our daughter should get a cochlear implant and that we should not sign with her so she focuses on listening. Is that right?
must_cover: Cochlear implants give partial and variable auditory access, not guaranteed language access
No evidence supports the claim that signing delays or harms spoken language
Bilingual-bimodal children with implants do as well as or better than implant-only children
Advice to withhold sign language is a red flag and deserves a second opinion
Sign language provides guaranteed access while the implant pathway develops
must_not: Signing will delay or harm the child's speech
A cochlear implant by itself settles how the child will learn language
Parents must choose either the implant or sign language but not both

question: People keep telling me my deaf son should know Deaf adults. Why does that matter, and how do we actually find Deaf mentors?
must_cover: Deaf mentors and fluent Deaf adults fill the language-quality gap while hearing parents are still learning ASL
Families can request Deaf mentor services through early intervention (the IFSP under IDEA Part C)
Meeting Deaf adults is one of the most informative things a new family can do
Deaf community events and Deaf mentor programs are concrete ways to connect
must_not: Deaf adults are irrelevant to a hearing family's decisions
Parents must be fluent signers before involving the Deaf community
Shaming the family for not having Deaf connections already

question: Our early intervention coordinator keeps talking about an IFSP meeting for our deaf baby. What is an IFSP, and what should we ask for in it?
must_cover: An IFSP is the Individualized Family Service Plan under IDEA Part C for children from birth to age three
It is family-centered and differs from the IEP that begins at age three
Families can ask for ASL or sign language services, Deaf mentors, and providers experienced with deaf children
Families have rights in the process, including evaluation and the right to disagree
Language access services should be in the written plan
must_not: The IFSP is only about hearing technology
Families have no say in what services are included
Fabricated statute numbers or legal specifics not present in the sources

question: My mother-in-law says that if we sign with our deaf toddler he will never learn to talk. Is there any truth to that?
must_cover: Research does not support the claim that sign language delays or prevents speech
Studies find early sign exposure has either no effect or a positive effect on spoken-language outcomes
The claim comes from oralist advocacy traditions rather than from data
A full first language during the critical period benefits the child regardless of which language they later prefer
must_not: Signing delays, harms, or replaces speech development
The child must pick one language or modality for life
Dismissing the grandmother's concern with ridicule instead of evidence

question: We are looking at school options for our deaf daughter. What does a school for the deaf actually offer that a mainstream classroom with an interpreter does not?
must_cover: Direct access to teachers and peers in a shared visual language, without waiting on an interpreter
Incidental and social learning throughout the school day, not just in lessons
An immersive signing environment is the central remediation for a child behind on language
Named examples exist, such as the Maryland School for the Deaf or the Clerc Center demonstration schools
Deaf schools pair ASL with English rather than rejecting speech or English literacy
must_not: Deaf schools reject English, speech, or literacy
Mainstreaming with an interpreter is always equivalent access
Fabricated enrollment numbers, dates, or program details not present in the sources

question: Our son is seven and we only started signing with him this year. I feel terrible that we waited. Is it too late for him?
must_cover: It is not too late: late sign exposure still improves language, behavior, and wellbeing
Language deprivation is usually the unintended outcome of well-intentioned choices, so the framing is forward-looking, not blaming
An immersive signing environment such as a Deaf school is the strongest remediation for a late start
Delayed language milestones are an emergency deserving immediate action, and acting now matters
Early exposure works best, so the family should escalate language access without delay
must_not: It is too late and nothing can be done
Shaming or blaming the parents for the late start
Claiming late exposure fully erases all effects of early deprivation

question: Are there national organizations that help families like ours with a deaf child, and what does each one actually offer?
must_cover: The National Association of the Deaf is the oldest US Deaf civil-rights organization and publishes positions relevant to deaf children and families
The Laurent Clerc National Deaf Education Center at Gallaudet offers national resources for families and runs the KDES and MSSD demonstration schools
The National Deaf Center focuses on postsecondary outcomes and offers transition resources and data useful to families
These national resources are available to families anywhere in the US, not only enrolled students
must_not: Families must pay for or enroll in these organizations to use their family resources
Fabricated program names, grant numbers, or founding dates not present in the sources
Only local audiology clinics can help a family
